An operator workspace for understanding paired-camera XYZ, inspecting rejection reasons and preparing a physical rig for possible future maze input.

Implementation PR · Issue #34 · Merged foundation PR #31

ChangeBehavior and evidenceChecks and reviewsScreenshotsPhysical follow-up

From a single-camera console to a rig workspace

The existing console answers single-view questions: what was detected, how fresh it is and whether its camera-local identity is usable. Coordinating a second angle adds distinct camera roles, metric geometry, exposure alignment and cross-view association. Placing all of that inside the existing console would make ordinary diagnostics harder to scan.

Recorded synthetic rehearsal

The new /rig.html page shows reference and supporting observations, their named anatomical joints, reconstructed X/Y/Z, a floor map and explicit unavailable states. Scenario and sample controls let an operator compare accepted estimates, rejection reasons and separate synthetic reference truth.

The committed dataset is generated by the existing Python XYZ solver, with semantic drift tests. Playback presents bounded recorded samples; browser animation is not pose inference or live capture.

Physical planning

Two independent named-device selectors assign stable camera roles, reject duplicate selections and recover from reordering or disconnection. Discovery is explicit and metadata-only. Existing selectors retain their default IDs and behavior.

Notes, intended placement and role-plan checks remain operator records. Switching out of rehearsal removes synthetic diagnostics; planning cannot make calibration, exposure timing, identity or maze input physically valid.

The work follows the user’s explicit choice of operator UI and synthetic rehearsal first. PR #31 was merged only after its latest-head checks were confirmed green. This follow-up uses a new branch and issue; it implements no maze gameplay or simultaneous live acquisition.

Actual solver outputs, explicit limits

Nine recorded cases contain eight samples each: 72 samples with 17 anatomical joints and two role-labelled source views. Source frames [0, 19, 38, 57, 75, 94, 113, 132] retain the complete 2.2-second movement span. They are generated by the existing midpoint solver; drift checks preserve metadata, nulls and reasons exactly with 1.1e-6 numerical rounding tolerance. The fixture shrank 33.3%, from 1,477,162 to 985,509 bytes, without removing a scenario, joint, quality gate or solver test. It establishes no physical accuracy.

A plausible two-view result can still have the wrong metric scale or identity. The hidden-bias case keeps this visible. A synthetic accepted sample is never labelled as physically validated or ready to control a maze.

Before and after, served locally

English desktop, mobile and narrow captures use actual Vite-served application code and styles. The baseline console entry source comes from merged commit 4bd2070, rendered with the current shared styles and runtime imports. Planning interactions use synthetic device metadata; no camera is opened.

What a physical maze input still needs

The current service supports one live source. A second call to its Start endpoint replaces that source; it does not create a calibrated camera pair. This workspace calls no capture endpoint and cannot convert existing host-read timestamps into verified exposure times.

A live implementation needs one owner per device, bounded pairing and source timing, scoped group lifecycle and partial-start cleanup, calibrated transforms tied to camera identities/image geometry, cross-view association and explicit missing/stale/recovery behavior. Independent held-out metric references, dynamic ground truth, overlap/play-boundary trials, useful update rate and external latency measurements must establish the declared rig’s limits before root XYZ controls a maze.
